history.p:
One of Georg Philipp Telemann’s last oratorios is his ‘Die Auferstehung’ to a text which he had commissioned from the poet Karl Wilhelm Ramler; the work was performed in Hamburg during Lent 1760. Soon afterwards Scheibe got hold of a copy of both Telemann’s new work as well as Ramler’s text, either through his correspondence with the composer or he might even have attended the first performance where he would have received the printed libretto together with the ticket. Scheibe was still living in the southern part of Denmark with easy access to Hamburg. Though the dating of Scheibe’s ‘Auferstehung’ is somewhat tricky, as the folios of the autograph manuscript have been trimmed with the loss of the last digit, it was certainly finished in the early 1760s. As with the previous oratorios, Scheibe also in the present one sought to put some of his theoretical ideas concerning the recitative and aria, for instance, into practice. Scheibe explained his ideas in great detail in three articles which appeared in 1764‒65 (SchW C1:Coll.001) and even discussed Telemann’s and Ramler’s new Passion oratorio concluding that 'this example is noble and sublime, and a sensitive listener will confirm this effect' (SchW C1:003, p. 235). However, in the same article Scheibe also includes a long music example which he copied from his own ‘Auferstehung’ (movement 12) ‒ though not mentioning the name of the composer ‒ explaining in detail the transitions between recitatives and accompagnato sections. Thus Scheibe composed the work sometime between 1760, when he might have got hold of the text, and 1764, when he employed various sections to illustrate his theoretical discussions. Scheibe refers again to his ‘Auferstehung’ in the article appearing the following year (SchW C1:004) and includes a music example from one of the recitatives (no. 18), and the final article from later that year (SchW C1:005) deals extensively with Ramler’s text. There is no evidence in terms of printed librettos that suggests that the work was ever performed in Copenhagen though there are clear indications in one of the manuscripts that the work was indeed performed.
It should be noted that two autograph manuscripts of Scheibe’s ‘Auferstehung’ have survived: one was clearly completed before the performance and should probably be defined as the composer’s working copy while the second manuscript is a fair copy of the first one. It is thought-provoking that Scheibe decided to produce a fair copy following the performance of the work – indeed, a practice which is seldom encountered among his contemporaries. It seems to have be a practice that he started on during the 1760s. Both manuscripts were acquired by Georg Poelchau in Berlin, for in 1829‒32 he writes to the court composer, C.E.F. Weyse, in Copenhagen looking for Scheibe manuscripts and mentions having received the ‘Auferstehung’.

Also letters nos. 213a (1 April 1829) and 214 (27 June 1829) mention Scheibe.

incipText.p: Gott! Du wirst seine Seele nicht in der Hölle lassen!
Mein Geist, voll Furcht und Freude, bebet
Die frommen Töchter Zions gehn verwundernd
Wer ist die Sionitinn, die vom Grabe so schüchtern
Freundinnen Jesu! sagt, woher so oft in diesen Garten?
Dort seh ich aus den Thoren Jerusalems
Triumph! Triumph! Der Fürst des Lebens sieget!
Mein Herr! mein Gott! mein Herr! mein Gott!
Triumph! Triumph! der Sohn des Höchsten sieget!

physDesc.watermark: emblem consisting of a coat-of-arms with a single diagonal band and the fleur-de-lis and the countermark 'IV' or 'VI' is partly visible. The same watermark is also seen in SchW B2:313 and B2:431 suggesting that all three works were most likely produced around the same time. Paper of a dense and rather coarse quality meaning that it is difficult to draw staves on the paper.
physDesc.physMedium: In 2o; upright format, originally consisting of nested bifolios; front flyleaf, title page (fol. 1r), blank page (fol. 1v), music (fols. 2r–74v; numbered 5–150 in ink (Scheibe)), blank folio with staves (fol. 75r–v), end board of original limp binding, end flyleaf; in all 75 folios. Scheibe’s numbering starting with 5 suggests that originally two folios were part of the source which might have been the upper limp board corresponding to the surviving end board. Hand-ruled paper, 16, 17, 18, 20, 21 staves (7 mm; single rastrum used) in dark brown ink and music in same or black ink; top and bottom staves have not been used. A clean autograph ink copy with only a few additions and corrections in ink, a single cancellation in ink. This source is an ink fair autograph copy of D-B, Scheibe 1b (Scheibe’s working copy), and might have been produced after the first performance (see note on final music page); furthermore, the additional choir sections, which are appended to Scheibe’s working copy, are included in the present source.

In modern full-binding with green boards and front and end flyleaves; the original lower board of a grey limp binding (same as in other works such as SchW B2:431) is included in the modern binding. The paste-down of the grey limp binding which has hand-ruled staves of the same ink and size suggests that this must once have been the original binding made when Scheibe had finished his copying. The upper board of the binding has not been preserved.
